concepts.title: Mahdism predates the third century AH
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari's historical argument begins by rejecting the idea that belief in Mahdism originated only around the birth of Imam al-Mahdi in the middle of the third century AH.

concepts.title: Qur'anic foundations
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari points to Qur'anic promises concerning the inheritance of the earth by righteous servants and the eventual triumph of true religion as general foundations for belief in a future righteous order.

concepts.title: Sunni as well as Shi'ah narrations
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari emphasizes that reports concerning the Promised al-Mahdi are not confined to Shi'ah collections; he cites the existence of substantial Sunni-source material as part of his historical argument.

concepts.title: The historical effect is the main question
concepts.explanation: Rather than simply cataloguing Qur'anic verses and hadith, Mutahhari says his principal concern is how belief in the Promised al-Mahdi affected Islamic history.

concepts.title: Imam 'Ali and the earth never being empty of God's proof
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari quotes the report of Imam 'Ali's conversation with Kumayl, emphasizing the principle that the earth is never empty of God's proof, whether that proof is manifest or hidden.

concepts.title: Mukhtar and the Mahdi claim
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari identifies Mukhtar's movement as an early historical example in which the Mahdi concept was used politically. Mukhtar presented Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah as the Promised Mahdi and himself as his representative.

concepts.title: The Kaysanite development
concepts.explanation: After Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah's death, followers associated with this movement maintained that he had not died and was hidden at Mount Radwa. Mutahhari presents this as part of the historical development of Mahdist ideas.

concepts.title: Zuhri's statement about the Ahl al-Bayt
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari cites Zuhri's reaction to Zayd ibn 'Ali's uprising as evidence that expectation of a future successful rising from the Prophet's family was already a recognizable idea in early Islamic discourse.

concepts.title: Nafs al-Zakiyyah and Mahdism
concepts.explanation: The chapter discusses Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah, known as Nafs al-Zakiyyah, and the way people connected claims about him with Mahdism because of lineage, name and other reported signs.

concepts.title: Imam al-Sadiq rejects a false Mahdi claim
concepts.explanation: When invited to support Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah's uprising, Imam al-Sadiq distinguished between supporting an uprising for enjoining good and forbidding evil and accepting the claim that Muhammad was the Promised Mahdi. He rejected the latter identification.

concepts.title: Why Mahdist claims repeatedly appeared
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari argues that the recurrence of Mahdist claims around various Alawi figures itself indicates how deeply established expectation of a future Mahdi was in the Muslim community.

concepts.title: The Abbasid use of the name al-Mahdi
concepts.explanation: The chapter notes that an Abbasid caliph was also named al-Mahdi, illustrating how the Mahdi concept had political and historical resonance beyond one specific doctrinal community.

concepts.title: Distinguishing historical claims from proof
concepts.explanation: A recurring exam point is that the existence of historical claims about a person being Mahdi does not itself prove the claim. Mutahhari distinguishes what people claimed from what he presents as the underlying doctrinal/historical evidence.

concepts.title: Mansur's political use of the Mahdi name
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari reports that Mansur named his son Mahdi and, according to the historical accounts he cites, sometimes used the name politically while privately acknowledging that neither his son nor 'Abd Allah al-Mahdi was the promised figure.

concepts.title: Muhammad ibn 'Ijlan's allegiance
concepts.explanation: The case of the Medinan scholar Muhammad ibn 'Ijlan illustrates the danger of confusing a claimant with the promised Mahdi. He pledged allegiance to 'Abd Allah al-Mahdi because he believed him to be the promised figure; scholars intervened on his behalf.

concepts.title: Early Muslim disputes were about identity, not existence
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari argues that early disagreements generally concerned which individual was the Mahdi, rather than whether the promised Mahdi existed at all. He cites disputes concerning Imam al-Kazim, Imam al-Baqir, Imam al-Sadiq and others.

concepts.title: Imam al-Sadiq and Isma'il's death
concepts.explanation: The chapter recounts how Imam al-Sadiq publicly demonstrated that his son Isma'il had died, specifically to prevent people from later claiming that Isma'il was the hidden Mahdi.

concepts.title: Di'bil's lamentation and Imam al-Rida
concepts.explanation: Di'bil recited a lamentation before Imam al-Rida naming tragedies suffered by the Ahl al-Bayt. Imam al-Rida added a reference to a grave in Tus, identifying it as his own future grave, and the poem also connected the history of suffering with the eventual reappearance of an Imam.

concepts.title: Mahdism as a Sunni historical phenomenon
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari argues that Mahdism cannot be treated as exclusively Shi'ah by pointing to Sunni populations and historical figures who accepted or claimed Mahdist ideas.

concepts.title: False Mahdis
concepts.explanation: The existence of false claimants is presented as another historical consequence of widespread belief in the promised Mahdi. Mutahhari distinguishes the existence of impostors from the truth of the underlying belief.

concepts.title: Historical references in Hafiz's poetry
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari notes Mahdist imagery in poems attributed to Hafiz, while explicitly saying he cannot establish whether Hafiz was Shi'ah or Sunni. The point is the presence of Mahdist expectation in Persian literary culture.

concepts.title: Reform is not the enemy of reappearance
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari addresses a dangerous interpretation: some people might think society must become maximally corrupt before the Imam can reappear, and therefore reform should be opposed. He rejects this reasoning.

concepts.title: The 'abscess' analogy
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari uses an abscess analogy to explain a revolutionary model in which accumulated corruption must reach a breaking point. He then contrasts this with the Islamic obligation to pursue reform rather than deliberately increase corruption.

concepts.title: Reappearance does not suspend religious duties
concepts.explanation: Waiting for Imam al-Mahdi does not cancel prayer, fasting, zakat, Hajj, enjoining good, forbidding evil, or other personal and social obligations. Mutahhari presents this as a direct rejection of passive or destructive interpretations of waiting.

concepts.title: Awaiting the Imam requires action
concepts.explanation: The correct expectation of reappearance is compatible with fulfilling religious duties and training individuals and society. The believer does not create corruption in order to accelerate the promised transformation.

concepts.title: The end of the historical discussion
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari closes the historical survey by moving from evidence for widespread Mahdist belief to the philosophical and practical meaning of awaiting the reappearance.

concepts.title: Justice after tyranny is not a command to produce tyranny
concepts.explanation: The promise that justice will follow oppression does not mean believers should permit or create oppression. The promised future is not a justification for abandoning present moral responsibility.

concepts.title: The core practical implication
concepts.explanation: The chapter connects Mahdism to active religious responsibility: personal worship, social obligations and moral reform remain valid while awaiting the Imam.

concepts.title: Core evidence chain
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari's historical chain is: Qur'anic promises → Prophetic reports → Imam 'Ali's statements → early Islamic Mahdist movements and claims → Sunni and Shi'ah historical evidence → practical meaning of awaiting reappearance.

concepts.title: Distinguish belief from political appropriation
concepts.explanation: A major exam distinction is between the doctrinal belief in a promised Mahdi and historical actors who appropriated the concept to legitimize political movements or particular claimants.

concepts.title: Distinguish evidence from interpretation
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari repeatedly separates historical reports from his interpretation of their significance. Statements such as why a claimant acted, whether someone privately believed a claim, or how a movement should be judged may remain matters of interpretation.

concepts.title: Overall conclusion of Chapter 8
concepts.explanation: The two-part chapter connects universal justice with Mahdism: justice is presented as the long-term direction of prophetic history, while the promised reappearance represents the culmination of that trajectory in a transformed human society.

concepts.title: Awaiting as faith and responsibility
concepts.explanation: The closing emphasis is that genuine awaiting is not passive pessimism. Mutahhari describes awaiting the reappearance as an expression of faith that coexists with worship, moral discipline, social responsibility and hope for humanity.
